title: Testing, code quality, and secure engineering
sources: Python 3.14 Standard Library: unittest, unittest.mock, tempfile, secrets, subprocess
pytest documentation concepts: fixtures, parametrization, assertions
OWASP guidance concepts: injection, input validation, secrets, deserialization
masterChecklist: Unit, integration, end-to-end, regression, property-based, and contract-test concepts
pytest: test discovery, assertions, fixtures, parametrization, mocks, temporary files, coverage
unittest, unittest.mock, test doubles, patching namespaces correctly
Static analysis, formatting, linting, type checking, documentation, code review
Security: input validation, injection risks, deserialization, path traversal, secrets, dependency risk, safe subprocess use
Accessibility, reliability, error messages, internationalization, privacy-aware logging
whyItMatters: Tests make a change safer, but only if they exercise a meaningful contract. Quality tooling catches cheap mistakes before review. Security work prevents untrusted input, paths, commands, and dependencies from turning a helpful script into a vulnerability.
simpleExplanation: A unit test checks a small behavior in isolation; integration tests check boundaries working together; end-to-end tests exercise a user-visible flow. A mock replaces a collaborator and should be patched where the code under test looks it up. Input validation checks shape and meaning before an action. Parameterized subprocess execution passes an argument list, not a shell command string.
mentalModel: A test suite is a set of safety rails for promises your code makes. Each rail should fail for the right broken behavior, not merely repeat the implementation. Security validation is a reception desk: it verifies who/what is allowed before sending anything into sensitive rooms.
outcomes: Choose a test level that matches a risk and write an assertion about behavior rather than private implementation.
Use pytest-style fixtures and parametrization conceptually, and recognize the equivalent unittest tools.
Patch the name used by the system under test, not the original module's name by habit.
Prevent common command injection and path traversal mistakes in file/CLI tools.
Describe why formatting, linting, type checking, review, and dependency updates are complementary rather than interchangeable.

realWorldExample.scenario: A document-conversion API accepts a user-selected file beneath an upload directory and calls a converter executable.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: Joining a raw path can escape the upload directory. Building shell=True command text can turn crafted input into another shell command. Tests that only mock the converter may never notice the boundary check is missing.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Resolve and verify the requested path remains below the trusted root, pass a list of fixed executable arguments to subprocess.run without shell=True, impose timeout/error handling, and test both allowed and rejected paths.

explanation: resolve normalizes .. segments and follows the platform's path resolution rules, allowing the program to compare complete paths.
The parent check rejects a candidate outside the trusted root. It is not enough to look for '..' in the original string.
subprocess.run receives a list, so Python invokes the program directly instead of asking a shell to parse user-controlled text.
check=True converts a nonzero converter exit into CalledProcessError; timeout prevents an indefinite wait.
The example still needs deployment-specific authorization, file-size policy, logging/redaction, and careful treatment of symlinks according to the environment.
workedExample.expectedOutput: safe_child(Path('uploads'), '../secret.txt') raises ValueError after the paths are resolved.
workedExample.safeExperiment: In a disposable practice directory, test report.txt and ../outside.txt. Do not run a real converter; replace the final call with print([...]) while learning.

procedure: Write an acceptance example first: input, expected outcome, and expected failure behavior.
Test pure rules as units; add integration tests around files, databases, and process boundaries using temporary resources.
Use fixtures to create known clean state and keep tests independent and repeatable.
Validate untrusted data early using allow-lists, size/type limits, and domain rules; avoid trusting file names or client claims.
Run formatter, linter, type checker, tests, and dependency/security review in the change workflow; investigate warnings rather than blindly suppressing them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Patching the library where it was defined instead of where the code under test imported it.
commonMistakes.why: The tested module may already hold a separate reference, so the mock has no effect and a real call leaks into the test.
commonMistakes.avoid: Patch the lookup name in the module under test, then assert the observable behavior.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using shell=True with an interpolated filename or user value.
commonMistakes.why: A shell interprets metacharacters, creating command-injection risk and platform-specific quoting bugs.
commonMistakes.avoid: Pass a list of arguments with shell=False; use a vetted library API where possible.

commonMistakes.mistake: Testing only happy paths or only mocked code.
commonMistakes.why: Boundary failures, malformed data, and integration assumptions are where production incidents occur.
commonMistakes.avoid: Include negative, boundary, and small integration tests with temporary resources.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating coverage percentage as proof of quality.
commonMistakes.why: A test can execute a line without checking its behavior; high coverage can still miss the important contract.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use coverage to find untested areas, then review assertions, mutation-risk cases, and user-visible outcomes.

lab.title: Test a safe filename boundary
lab.safety: This lab validates paths only. Do not execute system commands or use real upload data.
lab.starterCode:
from pathlib import Path

def allowed_file(root: Path, requested: str) -> Path:
    # TODO: resolve root and candidate
    # TODO: reject a candidate outside root
    # TODO: return the candidate only if it is a file
    pass
guidedSteps: Create a temporary root conceptually with a file named note.txt.
Resolve both root and root / requested before comparison.
Reject ../outside.txt with ValueError, not a generic filesystem failure.
Check is_file only after the containment check.
Write cases for note.txt, missing.txt, ../outside.txt, and a nested permitted filename.
checks: The code checks resolved paths, not string prefixes.
A filename containing a semicolon or spaces is treated as a filename, never as a command.
Missing and outside paths have distinct actionable failures.
The function performs no subprocess call.
hints: A child has root in candidate.parents; root itself should also be considered deliberately.
Use a separate is_file check after containment.

projectConnection.milestone: Build a test pyramid for the capstone: pure-rule unit tests, temporary-resource boundary tests, a small end-to-end happy path, documented lint/type/test checks, and an abuse-case review for input/path/subprocess handling.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: The project has reproducible tests, rejects untrusted boundary input safely, has no committed secrets, and explains the quality/security checks a contributor must run.

assessment.question: Where should a mock be patched?
assessment.answer: At the name lookup used by the code under test.
assessment.explanation: Patching the original library object may not replace a reference already imported into the module being tested.

assessment.question: Why is subprocess.run([...], shell=False) safer than shell=True with formatted text?
assessment.answer: The argument list avoids shell parsing of user-controlled characters.
assessment.explanation: It also avoids many quoting and portability problems.

assessment.question: What does high line coverage not prove?
assessment.answer: That the tests assert the important behavior, error cases, or real integration contract.
assessment.explanation: Coverage is a signal for investigation, not a guarantee of correctness.
